name: Exenatide

lead: Exenatide is the first GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for type 2 diabetes, in 2005. It is injected under the skin, either twice daily or once weekly.
It causes modest weight loss, but it is not approved for weight management and later GLP-1 drugs are reported to produce larger effects.

paras: It mimics GLP-1: it raises insulin release when glucose is high, lowers glucagon, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite. It is a synthetic version of a peptide found in Gila monster saliva.

The label warns of pancreatitis, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, kidney injury from dehydration and severe gastrointestinal effects. Nausea is common. It is prescription-only.

lead: Exenatide is a synthetic peptide that activates the GLP-1 receptor and is approved in the United States as an adjunct to diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes. It is based on exendin-4, a hormone first identified in the saliva of the Gila monster, and was first marketed as Byetta, a twice-daily injection, in 2005 [1][2][3]. An extended-release once-weekly form, Bydureon, followed [1].

Exenatide is not licensed for weight loss. Trial and review data describe a modest weight reduction in people with type 2 diabetes, with Grokipedia citing an average of 2 to 3 kg over six months [1]. It has since been overshadowed by later GLP-1 drugs such as liraglutide and semaglutide, which are reported to produce greater weight loss [2][4]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it appears mostly as an early example of the class, in 2005 to 2009 threads on T Nation [5][6][7].
infobox: Synthetic version of exendin-4 from Gila monster saliva [1]

paras: The US label for Byetta lists a single indication: adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, with coadministration with other exenatide products not recommended [3]. Grokipedia reports that the extended-release product is also indicated for patients aged 10 and above [1].

Weight loss is a known secondary effect. Researchers have used it as a model of GLP-1 action on appetite and reward areas of the brain [8]. A registered phase 4 trial examined exenatide and brown adipose tissue in obesity [9]. Off-label uses described in the literature include research in alcohol use disorder, idiopathic intracranial hypertension and Parkinson's disease, none of which relate to appearance [10][11][12].

Phase 3 trials added exenatide to metformin, sulfonylurea or both in type 2 diabetes and reported improved glycemic control with weight loss over 30 weeks [13][14][15]. Once-weekly exenatide was compared with twice-daily dosing in a non-inferiority study [16], and liraglutide once daily was compared with exenatide twice daily in LEAD-6 [4]. The EXSCEL trial assessed cardiovascular outcomes of once-weekly exenatide in type 2 diabetes [17], and meta-analyses of outcome trials report cardiovascular benefits across the GLP-1 class [18][19].

Trials outside diabetes include a randomized trial in alcohol use disorder [10], a trial in idiopathic intracranial hypertension [11], a trial in prediabetes with polycystic ovary syndrome comparing exenatide, metformin or both [20], and a Parkinson's disease trial published in The Lancet in 2017 [12]. Grokipedia reports that a later phase 3 trial found no disease-modifying benefit in Parkinson's disease [1]. Network meta-analyses compare glucose-lowering drugs, and one reviews fracture risk across anti-diabetic drugs [21][22]. Meta-analyses also cover liver outcomes and gastrointestinal events across the GLP-1 class [23][24].

The label warns of acute pancreatitis, hypoglycemia when used with insulin or insulin secretagogues, acute kidney injury from volume depletion, severe gastrointestinal reactions and immunogenicity, and states that pens must never be shared between patients [3]. Grokipedia lists nausea and vomiting among common effects, and thyroid C-cell tumor warnings in rodent studies [1]. Pregnancy data are limited, and animal studies have identified fetal and neonatal adverse effects [3].

Exenatide enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon and slows gastric emptying; its sequence partly overlaps with human GLP-1 [3][25]. It resists breakdown by DPP-4, which is why it lasts longer than native GLP-1, though the original product still needed twice-daily dosing [2][1].

Exendin-4 was identified in 1990, and Amylin Pharmaceuticals and Eli Lilly developed synthetic exenatide, according to Grokipedia [1]. Phase 3 registrations began in 2002 [26][27][28]. A 2005 T Nation thread discussed the approval of Byetta as a new diabetes drug derived from Gila monster saliva [6].

Forum discussion is sparse and dates mainly from 2005 to 2009. Posters speculated on its potential for fat loss, beta-cell effects and obesity treatment [7], and compared it with liraglutide and other drug classes [5].

lore.intro: Forum posts mention exenatide mainly as an early incretin drug and a possible fat-loss or beta-cell-supporting agent [6][7].
